evaluation.positioning_hook: A gifted Nairobi hacker is forced to steal a bank’s secret directory to save his parents, only to uncover a criminal dynasty built on his own family and a sister who may be the real power behind it.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clear commercial engine: a young hacker, a corrupt bank, a secret criminal network, and a family betrayal reveal that escalates into violence. The audience lane is real and legible, though the dense cyber-jargon and local specificity narrow the immediate mass-market read a bit.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: Mark is a hacker whose parents are arrested, then he’s coerced into stealing The Stylet Directory from Seraphic Bank. The premise keeps tightening as the sister, the Regency, and the double-crosses come into view.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Mark has a usable contradiction — arrogant, isolated, brilliant, and emotionally needy — and Tony gives him a workable foil. The supporting cast is vivid in function, but several characters are more plot-positioned than deeply individualized.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: A Kenyan cyber-crime thriller centered on family corruption and a hidden criminal syndicate is a fresher lane than the usual Western bank-heist template. The script is most distinctive when it leans into Nairobi texture, local institutions, and the family power structure.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps adding pressure: arrest, coercion, bank breach, betrayal, torture, and a final reveal about the sister and the Regency. The momentum is strong in the back half, though the opening stretches on banter and exposition before the main engine fully locks.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is fresh enough to stand out — a hacker pulled into a family criminal empire — but the execution often plays in familiar crime-thriller beats. The final reveal of the sister as Grand Regent gives it a sharper identity than the setup alone.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific world of Nairobi elites, legal institutions, cybercrime, bank security, and a hidden criminal organization with its own hierarchy. The Regency, Seraphic Bank, and the Masila family create a usable ecosystem with story-generating tension.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone mixes earnest family drama, pulpy crime, and broad banter, with occasional hard violence. That blend gives it personality, but the script sometimes swings between comic domestic sparring and grim thriller menace without a fully locked register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The sister disappearance, the parents’ hidden past, the Regency mythology, and the Kisumu references all suggest a deeper backstory beneath the surface plot. The script withholds enough to imply a larger conspiracy without feeling opaque.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Mark/Tony is a strong engine, and the family triangle with Rose and John gives the script recurring friction. Jackie, Bernard, Monica, Javan, and the bank-side players add enough relational pressure to keep the world active around the lead.

lead_characters.name: Mark Masila
lead_characters.hook: A brilliant, socially stunted hacker with a superiority complex and a real wound underneath it, Mark lives in his head and uses code as both weapon and armor. He starts as a smug loner helping people break into systems, then gets dragged into a family conspiracy that forces him to choose between ego, loyalty, and survival.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Riz Ahmed in The Night Of or a Rami Malek-style outsider lead — a role that lets an actor play intelligence, defensive humor, panic, and moral awakening in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Tony Baraka
lead_characters.hook: Tony is the polished, ambitious friend who can move between Mark’s world and the adult power structure with ease. He reads as the loyal big-brother figure until the script reveals he’s carrying his own agenda, which makes him one of the story’s most useful pressure valves and betrayals.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Mahershala Ali in Moonlight or Lakeith Stanfield in Judas and the Black Messiah a chance to be charming, ambiguous, and emotionally loaded without ever overexplaining himself.

lead_characters.name: Rose Masila
lead_characters.hook: Rose is the warm, sharp, quietly complicit mother who can switch from domestic mediator to technical co-conspirator in a beat. She’s the script’s clearest example of a parent whose love is real even when her ethics are compromised.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Viola Davis did in Fences or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk — authority, tenderness, and buried damage all at once.

lead_characters.name: John Masila
lead_characters.hook: John is the strict father whose moral language sounds principled until the family history starts to crack open. He’s intimidating, judgmental, and eventually revealed as part of a much larger criminal architecture, which gives him real late-story weight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the vein of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad’s early domestic scenes or Delroy Lindo in Da 5 Bloods — a role that lets an actor weaponize gravitas and then complicate it.

lead_characters.name: Sophie
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens/early 20s, Kenyan, law student
lead_characters.hook: Sophie is the hyper-competent, socially fluent counterpoint to Mark’s isolation, and she sees through him almost immediately. She’s witty, self-possessed, and emotionally direct, which makes her the script’s cleanest romantic and intellectual foil.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, scene-stealing role that gave Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Amandla Stenberg in Everything, Everything a chance to be smart, funny, and emotionally legible without being ornamental.

lead_characters.name: Jackson Owiro
lead_characters.hook: Owiro is the polished corporate patriarch who initially reads as a respectable boss and later reveals himself as Mr. Berk and a key node in the criminal network. The reveal gives him a double life that makes him one of the story’s most commercially useful villains.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal antagonist role that lets an actor do what Giancarlo Esposito did in Breaking Bad — charm first, menace later, with the audience recalibrating every scene.

lead_characters.name: Bernard Masawe
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Kenyan, bank executive, physical disability implied
lead_characters.hook: Bernard is a sadistic, theatrical power broker whose cane, temper, and appetite for control make him the story’s most overtly dangerous villain. He’s not subtle, but he is memorable, and the Double Roulette mythology gives him a signature that sticks.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain role that gives an actor the same kind of delicious, scene-devouring material that Javier Bardem had in No Country for Old Men or Ben Mendelsohn in Bloodline.

lead_characters.name: Monica
lead_characters.hook: Monica is the frightened insider whose trauma gives the bank plot its human cost. She’s not just a device; she’s the story’s clearest witness to Bernard’s abuse and the price of crossing him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but potent dramatic role in the vein of Carrie Coon in Gone Girl or Jodie Comer in The Last Duel — a character whose fear and testimony carry real emotional and plot weight.

lead_characters.name: Gordy
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens, Kenyan, tech helper
lead_characters.hook: Gordy is the eager junior hacker whose enthusiasm makes him useful and dangerous at the same time. He adds a younger, more naive energy to the hacking sequences and helps externalize Mark’s superiority complex.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that lets a young actor play comic eagerness, technical competence, and panic — the sort of part that often breaks out in ensemble crime pieces.

lead_characters.name: Javan Mutiso
lead_characters.hook: Javan is the smooth intermediary who moves information, pressure, and threats between the hidden players. He’s the kind of character who can disappear into a scene and still make it feel like the room has changed temperature.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic fixer role in the mold of Michael Kelly in House of Cards or Walton Goggins in Justified — controlled, slippery, and always one beat away from menace.

casting_characteristics: adult ensemble with several age-specific authority roles
lead requires strong tech dialogue delivery
villain roles benefit from strong physical presence

technical.vfx_details: primarily screen graphics, hacking interfaces, security feeds, and a few digital overlays
technical.sfx_needs: gunfire, practical blood effects, car explosion, broken glass, tactical raid elements

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with streamer-friendly crime-thriller positioning

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the SWAT raid, gun battles, car explosion, prison material, and multiple night exteriors push this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Mark needs a very specific blend of arrogance, vulnerability, and technical credibility, while Bernard and Jackie need strong villainous presence to make the final act land.

development.note: The script is carrying a lot of moving parts — the sister reveal, the Regency mythology, the Tony betrayal, the Mr. Berk/Owiro twist, and the parents’ hidden history — so the buyer conversation will center on clarity and consolidation.

comp_set.title: Blackhat
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the cyber-intrusion spine and the appeal of a gifted hacker pulled into a larger criminal system.

comp_set.title: Den of Thieves
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the muscular crime-thriller energy, law-enforcement pressure, and criminal-network escalation.

comp_set.title: The Accountant
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it centers an outsider with technical brilliance whose skills drag him into violent conspiracy.

comp_set.title: Searching
comp_set.why_it_comps: The missing-family-member engine and screen-native investigation give it a similar modern, tech-driven urgency.

comp_set.title: The Beekeeper
comp_set.why_it_comps: The revenge-through-corruption lane and the pleasure of a hidden system being exposed line up with the script’s escalation.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like propulsive crime thrillers with tech, corruption, and family betrayal at the center.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, male-leaning but workable for women who respond to high-stakes conspiracy and family drama; strongest with streaming audiences and genre fans.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary Nairobi settings, a modest VFX load, and a handful of action set pieces keep it in indie feature territory, though the raid and explosion sequences add pressure.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult, propulsive, corruption-driven lane where a strong lead and a clean hook can carry the package. The Nairobi setting and cybercrime angle give it a fresher international flavor without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the ending teases a larger world, but no clear spinoff vector is strong enough to justify franchise positioning.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A hacker thriller with family blood on it.
strengths.what_it_means: That combination gives the script a clean commercial identity: tech competence, criminal stakes, and emotional betrayal all in one package. Buyers looking for a genre movie with a human spine will see a lead role and a premise that can travel beyond the local market.
strengths.evidence: Mark’s hacking is tied directly to his parents’ arrest and the later reveal that the family is connected to The Regency.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Nairobi gives the story a real footprint.
strengths.what_it_means: The setting is specific enough to feel exportable rather than generic, which helps the script stand out in a crowded crime-thriller field. International buyers and streamers often respond to genre stories that feel locally rooted but globally legible.
strengths.evidence: The Masila home, Seraphic Bank, the courtroom, and the city streets all anchor the story in contemporary Nairobi.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Mark is a usable star-making lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actor arrogance, wit, technical fluency, emotional damage, and a late-story moral turn. That’s the kind of part that can attract a strong young performer and give a buyer a clear face for the campaign.
strengths.evidence: Mark’s dinner-table clashes, his date with Sophie, and his final confrontation with Jackie all expose different sides of him.

strengths.what_it_means: Bernard, Owiro, and Jackie create a layered antagonist field instead of a single-note bad guy. That gives the movie more packaging leverage because the threat can shift shape as the story unfolds.
strengths.evidence: Bernard’s Double Roulette speech, Owiro’s Berk reveal, and Jackie’s final cemetery confrontation all reframe the power structure.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The back half has real escalation.
strengths.what_it_means: Once the bank hack, Monica’s death, and the warehouse showdown kick in, the script becomes a true pressure cooker. That kind of escalation is what turns a premise into a trailerable movie.
strengths.evidence: The bank breach, Bernard’s torture scene, the car ambush, and the final cemetery reveal all keep raising the stakes.

whats_special.headline: This is a commercially legible Nairobi-set cybercrime thriller with a strong young lead, a family-conspiracy hook, and enough villainous texture to feel bigger than a standard hack-and-chase movie. It’s also producible at an indie feature level, which makes it attractive to streamer buyers looking for elevated genre without tentpole spend.

items.area: The opening spends a long time explaining the hacker.
items.detail: The first stretch is heavy on technical dialogue and domestic banter before the central coercion engine fully takes over. That’s not a fatal flaw, but it does delay the moment a buyer feels the movie’s main promise snap into place.

items.area: The conspiracy stack gets crowded fast.
items.detail: By the back half, the script is juggling the parents’ fraud case, the Regency, Mr. Berk/Owiro, Tony’s hidden allegiance, Jackie’s reveal, and Bernard’s separate power base. That density gives the world scope, but it also creates a development conversation about how much explanation the audience is expected to carry.

items.area: Bernard’s violence is a buyer-sensitive lane choice.
items.detail: The Monica execution and the torture beats push the material into hard-R territory with explicit sadism. That’s workable for streaming and some genre buyers, but it narrows the theatrical conversation and makes tone management a real packaging factor.

items.area: Tony’s turn needs a very specific read.
items.detail: He functions as Mark’s emotional anchor, then becomes part of the hidden machinery, then returns as a rescue figure. That makes him valuable, but it also means the casting and performance have to preserve trust even when the script withholds his full agenda.

items.area: The cyber dialogue narrows the audience a bit.
items.detail: Terms like ARP tables, MAC addresses, rootkits, and decryption keys give the movie texture, but they also ask the audience to track a lot of process. For some buyers that reads as specificity; for others it reads as friction against the broader thriller promise.

issues.headline: The main friction is not premise — it’s density. The script has a strong hook and a marketable lead, but the layered conspiracy, technical dialogue load, and hard-R violence will be the first things a producer weighs before saying yes.
